items.title: Buddy DeFranco interviewed by Monk Rowe, Sarasota, Florida, April 13, 1996
items.q: I still am, well with a recommendation from Stan Kenton... Stan says “well that’s true, things are bad, why don’t you do what I do? Let’s get into the schools... We know we’re not going to do much good with the older people, but let’s get in the schools and get the young people and see what we can d

ctx.x: So shortly after that group, Basie was able to, economically I guess, add his people back.

There again, Willard Alexander said the time now is right for the big band and I think Bill Basie is the kind of a guy that could spearhead this kind of thing, and he knew he had Joe Williams with Basie’s band, who was a plus factor, not only musically but commercially. And he said to Bill Basie, “Time for the big band.” And everybody in the business, including Norman Granz, said better not take a chance, you know. Big bands are finished. But Willard said no, let’s go ahead, let’s go ahead. And they did and they…
You got into some jazz education early on.

items.title: DeFranco Buddy — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I ran into Stan Kenton one time, and I was bemoaning the fate of jazz... And Stan said, 'You should do what we’re doing.'

ctx.x: That was in ’46. So you had left Tommy Dorsey…
Right, I must have been in California…
Murphy:…and it was a pretty short lived experience, right?
